notes: No sentence reports a bilingual, a glossary or expected names held on outside grounds, and none states their absence. Inscription l has a hieratic part read as an Egyptian dating formula, but the account does not call it a version or a name.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: The Udi language, spoken by some 8,000 people, mostly in the Republic of Azerbaijan but also in Georgia and Armenia, is considered to be the last direct continuator of the Caucasian Albanian language.
CORPUS_quote: Between 1947 and 1952, archaeological excavations at Mingachevir under the guidance of S. Kaziev found a number of artifacts with Caucasian Albanian writing, namely a stone altar post with an inscription around its border that consisted of 70 letters, and another 6 artifacts with brief texts (containing from 5 to 50 letters), including candlesticks, a tile fragment, and a vessel fragment.
notes: Outside grounds: a living descendant (Udi) and early tradition (Koriun, Movses Kaghankatvatsi) naming the Albanian language; script 'mentioned in early sources' before 1937. The account does not say in so many words what scholars held in 2001. Only figures given: 70 letters plus 6 texts of 5 to 50 letters, so at most about 370. No size is given for the Sinai palimpsest (found after T).

The account says the coins' reverse is 'in Pali' and that the script was once called 'Arian-Pali', but does not report that scholars at 1837 held a language identification on stated outside grounds, nor that the language was unknown.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: The use of the Libyco-Berber alphabet died out in northern areas during or after the reign of the Roman Empire and Byzantine Empire, but it spread south into the Sahara desert and evolved there into the Tuareg Tifinagh alphabet used by the Tuareg Berbers to this day.
notes: Low confidence. Outside ground in the account: living descendant script used by Tuareg Berbers, and Berber peoples of the place; family named is Berber. The account does not say what scholars held in 1843; a strict reading gives NS.

VALUES_quote: According to François Desset, the scholar who deciphered this writing, Linear Elamite was created in a completely autonomous way with respect to the cuneiform, the Mesopotamian writing system that was widespread in the Near East, including the Elamic region.
notes: From the Mnamon account. The only resemblance reported is to Proto-Elamite, which is not a readable script.

ANCHOR_quote: Specifically, there are several inscriptions in Lycian and Greek, mainly used in the dedicatory inscriptions of tombstones.
notes: From the Mnamon account. The account does not date the discovery of these bilinguals against 1821 (it says many inscriptions were recorded by travellers in the nineteenth century; the Xanthos pillar was first published 1843).
Mnamon gives a count ('a hundred inscriptions') but no typical length in signs; it says most are a single word and also that most are funerary, so no product can be formed.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: Although the Maya did not actually write alphabetically, nevertheless he recorded a glossary of Maya sounds and related symbols, which was long dismissed as nonsense (for instance, by leading Mayanist J. E. S. Thompson in his 1950 book Maya Hieroglyphic Writing) but eventually became a key resource in deciphering the Maya script.
WORDDIV_quote: Maya texts were usually written in blocks arranged in columns two blocks wide, with each block corresponding to a noun or verb phrase.
notes: Outside ground: Landa's colonial-era record tying the glyphs to Maya sounds, plus continuous use in the Maya Lowlands until the conquest. The account does not state outright which language scholars assumed in the 1950s. Regular visual unit is the glyph block; the account equates a block with 'a noun or verb phrase', not strictly a word.

WORDDIV_quote: A graph when inverted horizontally generally refers to the same word, and additional components are sometimes present without changing the meaning.
notes: Read as one sign per word (also 'representing concepts exclusively through words'). The account has no explicit statement about word division, so NS is the strict alternative.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: As the language and script of religious and semi-religious commentaries, Pahlavi remained in use long after that language had been superseded (in general use) by Modern Persian and Arabic script had been adopted as the means to render it.
notes: Outside ground: continuous Zoroastrian tradition down to the 17th century, tying the script to (Middle) Persian. The account does not say outright what de Sacy assumed.

ANCHOR_quote: KAI 277: Pyrgi Tablets, Phoenician-Etruscan bilingual, c. 500 BC
notes: Low confidence. The quote is a list entry, not a full sentence. The account lists bilinguals (Karatepe, Pyrgi, Cinekoy) but gives no discovery dates, does not say which objects the 1758 decipherment used beyond naming the Cippi of Melqart, coins and Kition inscriptions, and does not call the Cippi bilingual. Strict alternative: NS.

CORPUS_quote: The Proto-Sinaitic script is a Middle Bronze Age writing system known from a small corpus of about 30–40 inscriptions and fragments from Serabit el-Khadim in the Sinai Peninsula, as well as two inscriptions from Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt.
notes: Count times length: about 30-40 inscriptions; lengths given are 'three, four signs' for some (Mnamon) and 16 and 12 characters for Wadi el-Hol; 40 x 16 = 640, under 1,000. No single typical length is stated ('some are longer').

ANCHOR_quote: Guy suggests syllabic readings for some of these, based on possible rebuses and correspondences with the names of the nights in the old calendar.
VALUES_quote: Thus rongorongo appears to have been an internal development.
WORDDIV_quote: Fischer notes that the long text of the 125-cm Santiago Staff is unlike other texts in that it appears to have punctuation: The 2,320-glyph text is divided by "103 vertical lines at odd intervals" which do not occur on any of the tablets.
notes: Low confidence. No readable parallel text (the account lists 'the lack of context ... such as illustrations or parallel texts which can be read' as an obstacle; the Jaussen list 'has not led to an understanding'). Expected names: night names of the lunar month recorded by Thomson, sought in the Mamari calendar. These are calendar names, not rulers, places or gods; alternative code 0. Only resemblance claimed is to the Indus Valley script, itself undeciphered and described as debunked. Only the Staff has dividing lines, and they mark sections of several glyphs, not words. If those were taken as word division the code would be 1.

ANCHOR_quote: In a few instances, shell inscriptions are paired with Brāhmī letters, as in the example at Deogarh, Uttar Pradesh, illustrated here.
notes: Low confidence. The account says shell inscriptions are paired with Brahmi but does not say the Brahmi repeats the shell text or name.

LANG_PRIOR_quote: According to the History of Song (1346), the script was designed by the high-ranking official Yeli Renrong in 1036.
LANG_HIND_quote: The Tangut script is a logographic writing system, formerly used for writing the extinct Tangut language of the Tanguts.
ANCHOR_quote: Official documents were written in the script (with diplomatic ones written bilingually).
notes: Outside ground: Chinese historical record tying the script to the Western Xia (Tangut) state; language named as Tangut. The account does not describe what scholars held in the 1930s. The account calls the language extinct and names no known language or close relative; coded under 'else 0'. NS is the strict alternative. Also scriptures translated from Tibetan and Chinese. The account does not date when such bilingual material reached scholars.

ANCHOR_quote: In this tablet every Ugaritic consonant is “translated” into an Akkadian syllabic sign which should render its pronunciation.
notes: From the Mnamon account (abecedary KTU 5.14; also polyglot lists with a Ugaritic column). The account does not date these finds against 1930.
